I suspect as our logs and response codes indicate, the resources were all created properly, but the update to the parents listing of children got trampled. Assume they all pass, as they have on the branch of code against which they were written.  If you discover that they wouldn't pass under certain circumstances, document those as bugs and @ignore the test that identifies said circumstances.

I understand the tests now are crude.  The goal of them is to ensure that two roughly concurrent operations proceed with predictable results.  In theory we'd need to test for scheduling that switches at literally every point in the running code to fully test it.  I don't know what options Awaitility offers, or what's practical.  Assuming you have the ability to ensure that scheduling of one thread is deferred until another processes and is blocked, I'd recommend testing with such switch points right before and right after any instances of lock acquisition or session granting/saving, as those would seem like the edge cases.
Then I don't understand the import of the error report above. Does it not clearly demonstrate a failure of these very tests in just the case in which you say they don't fail?

The above report was only observed when backporting to a previous release.  Lots of other differences existed, and the limitation of the current integration testing made it difficult to determine if it was a bug that affects the current codebase, or one that had been fixed between 4.6 and 4.7.  I thew it out there as an example of something I'd hope an improved integration test framework could answer.
Okay, that makes more sense. In that case, I understand the need here simply to be to check that two concurrent requests to create the same resource both proceed, one failing and one succeeding?
How can I check that the test fails in the absence of your fix (i.e. is there a commit I can revert)?
I've made a dummy PathLockManager implementation that does nothing to see the failures or commented out the code that acquires the lock.

Reopening this ticket because we will want to ensure that these scenarios work correctly even in the case that the locking code is refactored into the kernel layer, per:

All of them have the basic pattern that we start a bunch of thread that perform concurrent operations at roughly the same time and make sure they do the appropriate things.  In practices these tests consistently failed without the concurrency fix and always passed with the fix, but there's no guarantee they'll fail even without concurrency control depending on variations on the thread scheduling in the machine on which the tests are running.

Apparently there are fancy frameworks that will allow us to elevate these tests from smoke-tests to something that will actually make assertions about our code in hypothetical but precise concurrency scenarios.

renderedFields.description:
FedoraLDPIT contains the following tests:

testConcurrentPuts
testConcurrentPutsWithPairtrees
testConcurrentUpdatesToBinary
testConcurrentPatches

All of them have the basic pattern that we start a bunch of thread that perform concurrent operations at roughly the same time and make sure they do the appropriate things. In practices these tests consistently failed without the concurrency fix and always passed with the fix, but there's no guarantee they'll fail even without concurrency control depending on variations on the thread scheduling in the machine on which the tests are running.

Apparently there are fancy frameworks that will allow us to elevate these tests from smoke-tests to something that will actually make assertions about our code in hypothetical but precise concurrency scenarios.
